dek: Halloween, the time change, and why grown adults keep masking as the year turns dark.

slides.label: Double Hour
slides.text: Halloween night bled into a *25 hour day*: at 2 a.m. the clocks fell back, and *one hour happened twice*.

slides.label: Ancient Roots
slides.text: Halloween traces back to *Samhain*, a Celtic festival where the dead were believed to cross into the living world.

slides.label: Hallowtide
slides.text: The Church built *All Saints' and All Souls' Days* onto the old calendar, creating a season called *Hallowtide*.

slides.label: Latin America
slides.text: In Latin America Halloween is the guest: Nov 1 honors the *angelitos*, children who died; Nov 2 honors the adults.

slides.label: Global Dead
slides.text: From Haiti's *Fèt Gede* to Guatemala's giant kites to Bolivia's *decorated skulls*, the dead get their own days worldwide.

slides.label: The Cost
slides.text: The clocks falling back isn't just an extra hour of sleep: studies link it to an *11% jump* in new depression cases.

slides.label: Grown Folks Take Over
slides.text: In 2026, adults spent *$2 billion* on costumes, more than on kids, a shift rooted in *queer nightlife* of the 1970s.

slides.label: Beyond the Mask
slides.text: Long before stores sold skeleton suits, traditions like Lucumí's *egun* and the *barón del cementerio* kept the dead close all year.

caption_instagram:
This Halloween, the clocks didn't just fall back, they folded time in half: at 2 a.m. on November 1, one hour happened twice, right as the veil between Halloween and Día de los Muertos thins.

That extra hour is old magic in a new outfit. The Celts called it Samhain. The Church turned it into All Saints' and All Souls' Days. Latin America turned it into a three day season where Nov 1 belongs to the angelitos and Nov 2 belongs to the adults, while Haiti's Fèt Gede, Guatemala's giant kites and Bolivia's decorated skulls all keep their own dead close.

Meanwhile adults in the U.S. spent $2 billion dressing up this year, more than they spent on their kids, proof the mask stopped being a kid's game decades ago in queer nightlife and never looked back.

Halloween just gave us a lesson in timing. At 2 a.m. on November 1, the clocks fell back and one hour happened twice, a 25 hour day lining up with centuries of ritual around endings and renewal.

For builders, the real story is the Village Halloween Parade. It started in 1974 as a small puppet procession for kids in Greenwich Village, built by a community, New York's queer nightlife, that needed one night to be fully itself. Everyone else eventually asked to come in. That is how culture actually scales: build something real for your own people first, until it's too good to ignore.

Forty-seven percent of shoppers used AI to plan this year's costumes, and American adults spent $2 billion on their own outfits, more than on their kids'. The mask used to hide you. Now it's how you get seen.
